Chapter 5. Compassion, Change, and Living Without Free Will.
Letting go of the idea of free will? That’s not exactly something that comes naturally. It goes against what we feel in our gut, what our culture tells us, and even the stories we use to make sense of who we are. But if you’re willing to really lean into this truth, something amazing can happen—it can change the way you see your whole life.
Picture a teacher in a classroom, dealing with a student who’s always acting out. For years, the story has been simple: this kid is just lazy, or maybe stubborn—choosing to misbehave. But what if there’s another way to see it? Maybe that student is shaped by things we don’t see—family problems, learning struggles, or just needs that haven’t been met yet. Suddenly, the teacher’s response shifts. Instead of punishment and frustration, there’s support. Instead of anger, there’s genuine empathy.
The same thing happens in our close relationships. Say a friend lets you down. It’s so easy to feel hurt, or even betrayed, and think they could’ve chosen differently. But when you realize their actions were shaped by forces outside their control, forgiveness becomes a little easier. The weight of blame lifts, and what’s left is understanding—and a deeper kind of compassion.
Now, think about how this perspective changes how we see ourselves. So many of us wrestle with stubborn habits: procrastination, overeating, anxiety—the list goes on. The old story is that it’s just weakness, or that we’ve somehow failed. But with a new lens, we start to see how powerful habits are, how much biology and luck matter. Change isn’t about beating ourselves up. It’s about understanding, patience, and a little more kindness toward ourselves.
Living without the illusion of free will doesn’t mean we stop trying to change or that we dodge responsibility. People still set goals, make plans, and work hard. But now, we see it as part of a bigger web—a chain of causes and effects. Success becomes something to celebrate, but not a reason to feel superior. And when we fall short, there’s compassion instead of shame.
This approach isn’t passive or hopeless. In fact, it’s the opposite. It’s active, it’s engaged, and it’s grounded in reality. It recognizes what’s beyond our control, but also the power of understanding and support. When we see the world clearly, instead of how we wish it would be, whole new possibilities open up—for growth, for connection, and for genuine kindness.
Making the leap from believing in free will to truly understanding the mind? It isn’t easy. It challenges a lot of what we hold dear and asks us to be humble. But if you stick with it, you might just find a path to something more freeing—a life with less judgment, more compassion, and a deeper sense of what it means to be human.
